lessonTitle: Communication, Teamwork and Teaching: Patients, the Multidisciplinary Team and Junior Colleagues

blocks.text: A 74-year-old man is being discharged after starting a new medicine for atrial fibrillation. The nurse says he nodded through your explanation, and an hour later the pharmacist finds he thinks the tablet is 'for his chest' and plans to take it only when he has symptoms. Nobody was careless; the explanation was simply never checked. Most communication failures look like this: information was sent but not received.

blocks.markdown: Communication is a clinical skill with its own technique, and in a hospital it is the main route by which errors are either caught or created. In this unit you will use three layers: communicating with **patients and relatives**, communicating and working with **colleagues in the multidisciplinary team**, and **teaching and giving feedback** to more junior colleagues and students. The same principles run through all three: be clear, be brief, check that the message has landed, and show respect for the other person's role and knowledge.

blocks.title: Teach-back
blocks.text: A way of checking understanding in which you ask the listener to explain the information in their own words, framed as a test of your explanation rather than of them (for example, 'I want to be sure I explained this clearly; can you tell me how you will take this medicine?'). If the explanation is wrong, you re-explain differently and check again.

rows: Start with 'tell me about...' then narrow with specific questions
Say what you will cover and give information in small pieces
Patient restates the information in their own words
After any explanation, especially medicines or discharge advice
A trained interpreter, in person, by phone or video
Whenever there is a language barrier; avoid using relatives for clinical communication
Escalation and handover calls to colleagues
The receiver repeats back an instruction and the sender confirms
blocks.caption: Common communication tools and when to use them.

blocks.markdown: **With patients and relatives.** Introduce yourself with your name and role, wash your hands, and check you have the right patient. Ask permission to ask questions, sit at the same level, listen without interrupting and use plain words in place of jargon: 'blood thinner' rather than 'anticoagulant' at first, and then the proper name. Explore the patient's ideas, concerns and expectations. Give information in small pieces, check understanding, and finish by summarising and agreeing the next steps. For consent and confidentiality, the General Medical Council's guidance applies; check the current version.

blocks.title: Explaining a new medicine with teach-back
blocks.prompt: A 74-year-old man is being discharged with a new blood-thinning tablet because of atrial fibrillation. Show how you would explain it and check understanding.

steps.text: Prepare and set the scene: sit down, ask what he already knows ('What did the doctors tell you about your heart rhythm?'), and say you will cover what the tablet is for, how to take it and what to watch for.

Give the information in chunks using plain language: 'Your heart rhythm is irregular, which lets clots form. This tablet lowers the risk of a clot and a stroke. It must be taken every day, not only when you feel unwell.'

Name the main safety messages without overload: report black stools, unusual bruising or bleeding, and tell any doctor or dentist that he takes it. Say that the exact drug and dose are on his pharmacy label and should be checked against current BNF and local guidance by the prescriber.
Use teach-back: 'I want to be sure I explained this well. Can you tell me in your own words what the tablet is for and when you will take it?'

Respond to what you hear: if he says he will take it when his chest feels odd, correct this kindly, re-explain with a different image ('like an umbrella you keep up every day') and check again, then give written information and document the discussion.

blocks.answer: He should be able to state the purpose, the daily timing and one warning sign. If the answer is wrong, the explanation, not the patient, is revised and the check is repeated.

blocks.markdown: **With colleagues.** Medical care is delivered by teams, and errors usually arise at the interfaces. Address people by name, state who you are and what you need, and use SBAR for urgent calls. Closed-loop communication reduces misheard instructions: 'Please give 500 mL of fluid over 15 minutes' is answered 'Giving 500 mL over 15 minutes, confirmed' (an illustrative instruction only; volumes and rates must be checked against current guidance and local policy). Treat every professional group as a source of expertise, and thank colleagues for catching errors. If a concern remains, say so directly and politely, for example by stating what worries you and what you need.

rows: Trends, concerns and what has changed since the last review
Medicines reconciliation, interaction and dose checks, supply
Formulary choices, renal dosing, unavailable drugs
Function in daily living, home assessments, adaptations
Whether a patient can manage at home
Safe diet and fluids, alternative communication
Condition-specific expertise (for example diabetes, stroke, palliative care)
blocks.caption: Roles in the multidisciplinary team: who to ask and why.

blocks.markdown: **Referral etiquette.** A good referral gets the right person to see the right patient at the right time. Decide the question first: what do you want the other team to do? Check the patient's details, location and the relevant history, observations and results, and make sure the basic tests the specialty expects have been done. Tell the patient why you are referring them. State the urgency honestly, name the consultant you are working for, and be polite and brief. If you phone, use SBAR and end with a clear request. Record the referral, the person you spoke to, the time and the advice. If the other team declines, ask politely for their reasons, clarify the question and, if you are still concerned, take it to your own senior to discuss with their senior rather than letting the patient fall between teams.

blocks.title: Making a non-urgent specialty referral
blocks.prompt: A 68-year-old man on a medical ward has unexplained weight loss over 3 months and a haemoglobin of 78 g/L with a low mean cell volume and low ferritin, a pattern consistent with iron-deficiency anaemia. He is haemodynamically stable. Outline an effective referral to gastroenterology.

steps.text: Define the question: 'Please advise on investigation of suspected gastrointestinal blood loss or malignancy in a man with iron-deficiency anaemia and weight loss.'

Prepare the details: patient name, hospital number, ward and bed, observations, haemoglobin, mean cell volume, ferritin and other blood tests already done, medicines (noting any anticoagulant or antiplatelet), and his consultant.
Tell the patient about the referral and the reason, and check his agreement and wishes.
Make the request through the agreed route (an electronic referral or a call) using SBAR, and state the urgency as soon but not emergency since he is stable.
Document the referral, who accepted it, the time, any advice (for example further tests to be done in the meantime) and your plan to follow up, then hand over the outstanding actions.

blocks.answer: A well-formed referral has a clear question, identifiers and relevant data, patient awareness, an honest urgency, a named senior, documentation and follow-up.

blocks.markdown: **Teaching and feedback.** Teaching is part of a doctor's professional role, and the General Medical Council expects doctors to contribute to the education of students and colleagues where appropriate. Effective bedside teaching starts with what the learner already knows, sets a small goal, uses the real patient or task, and ends with feedback. Feedback is information about what the learner did, compared with a standard, that helps them improve. It works best when it is timely, specific, based on observed behaviour, balanced and actionable, and offered in private and with respect. The widely used 'one-minute preceptor' model gives five steps.

items: Get a commitment: ask the learner what they think is going on or what they would do.
Probe for supporting evidence: ask why, to uncover their reasoning.
Teach a general rule: give one or two take-home points.
Reinforce what was done well, naming the behaviour.
Correct mistakes: describe the error and what to do next time, then check understanding.

blocks.title: Feedback that does not help
blocks.text: 'Well done' and 'you need to be more confident' are too vague to change behaviour. Comments about personality ('you are careless') provoke defensiveness. Describe what you saw and its effect, for example 'you did not wash your hands before touching the patient; next time clean them before and after the examination'. Do not leave serious safety concerns until a scheduled meeting; deal with them at once.

points: Check that your message has been understood: use teach-back with patients and closed-loop communication with colleagues.
Use professional interpreters rather than relatives for clinical communication when there is a language barrier.
Know what each member of the multidisciplinary team does, and refer with a clear question, relevant data, an honest urgency and documentation.
Teach from the learner's level and give timely, specific, behaviour-based feedback; the one-minute preceptor is a practical bedside structure.

questions.stem: You have explained a patient's new discharge medicines to her. Which is the best way to check that she has understood?

options.text: Give her a leaflet and move on
Repeat the explanation more slowly in the same words
Ask 'Do you understand?' and accept her nod
Ask her to explain in her own words how she will take each medicine

questions.correctOptionText: Ask her to explain in her own words how she will take each medicine

distractorRationale.a: Written material helps but does not confirm understanding.
distractorRationale.b: Does not test whether she has understood.
distractorRationale.c: Patients often nod out of politeness.

questions.explanation: Teach-back asks the patient to demonstrate what they have understood, and treats any mistake as a flaw in the explanation to be fixed. A nod or a leaflet alone does not show that the message has been received.

questions.stem: A patient who speaks Polish and very little English needs to be told about an operation. His adult son, who speaks English well, offers to interpret. What is the best approach?

options.text: Use simple English and gestures to avoid delay
Ask a nurse who knows a little Polish to help informally
Use a professional interpreter, and involve the son in other ways if the patient wishes
Let the son interpret because he knows the patient best

questions.correctOptionText: Use a professional interpreter, and involve the son in other ways if the patient wishes

distractorRationale.c: Correct: accuracy, impartiality and confidentiality are protected.
distractorRationale.d: Risks omissions, distortion and the patient withholding information.

questions.explanation: Professional interpreters are trained to translate accurately and impartially and to preserve confidentiality, and relatives may filter or alter the content. Family members can still be present if the patient wants, but should not be relied on for clinical interpretation.

questions.stem: A nurse phones you with a verbal request to stop a patient's intravenous infusion and to recheck her observations in 30 minutes. What is the best way to reduce the chance of a misunderstanding?

options.text: Ask her to write it on a sticky note instead
Repeat the instruction back to the nurse and ask her to confirm that it is correct
Wait until the end of your shift to write it down
Say 'OK' and hang up quickly to save time

questions.correctOptionText: Repeat the instruction back to the nurse and ask her to confirm that it is correct

distractorRationale.a: Informal and not part of the record.
distractorRationale.c: Delays documentation and increases the risk of error.

questions.explanation: Closed-loop communication means the receiver repeats back the message and the sender confirms it, which catches mishearing and ambiguity. It should be followed by documentation in the notes or the electronic system.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old man after a stroke coughs when drinking water, and the ward team asks who should assess his swallow and advise on the safest diet and fluids. Which team member is most appropriate?

options.text: The speech and language therapist
The social worker
The physiotherapist
The occupational therapist

distractorRationale.d: Assesses daily function and the home environment, not the swallow.

questions.explanation: Speech and language therapists assess swallowing and advise on diet and fluid consistency, as well as communication difficulties after stroke. Other therapists contribute in different ways, but not to swallow assessment.

questions.stem: You need to refer a patient to the on-call specialty team. Which of the following best describes an effective referral?

options.text: Refer before any investigations so they can decide everything themselves
Wait for the consultant to call you if they are interested
Ask them to 'just come and have a look' without detail
State identifiers and location, the specific question and urgency, the relevant history and results, and what has already been done, after telling the patient

questions.correctOptionText: State identifiers and location, the specific question and urgency, the relevant history and results, and what has already been done, after telling the patient

distractorRationale.a: Teams expect basic work-up unless urgent.
distractorRationale.c: Does not state a question or urgency.

questions.explanation: A good referral makes it easy for the other team to act: it states what you want, how urgent it is and gives the key data. The patient should know and agree to the referral, and you should document who accepted it and what advice was given.

questions.stem: You phone the on-call team of another specialty about a patient you consider needs review today. The registrar says 'this is not our problem, ring the medical team'. You remain worried about the patient. How should you respond and what steps should you take?
markingGuide: Stays calm and professional; restates the specific clinical question and the reason for concern
Provides key data using SBAR and asks what additional information would help
Politely asks the registrar to explain their reasons and whether there is a different route
If still concerned, escalates to own registrar or consultant to speak to the other consultant, rather than letting the patient fall between teams
Keeps patient safety paramount and continues initial management meanwhile
Documents the call (time, name, advice, outcome) and the plan, and informs the nurse in charge
Avoids blame and treats the other team respectfully
questions.explanation: The key principle is that the patient must not be left without a responsible team. A good answer shows professional courtesy, clarity of the clinical question, the use of the chain of command and clear documentation.

questions.stem: In the 'one-minute preceptor' teaching model, what is the first step after the learner presents a case?

options.text: Give them the correct diagnosis straight away
Ask them to commit to an opinion, for example what they think is going on
Summarise the general rule
Correct their mistakes in front of the patient

questions.correctOptionText: Ask them to commit to an opinion, for example what they think is going on

distractorRationale.c: The general rule follows probing for reasoning.
distractorRationale.d: Correction comes later and in private.

questions.explanation: The first step is to get a commitment, which reveals what the learner already thinks and engages them actively. Probing, teaching a rule, reinforcing and correcting follow in turn.

questions.stem: A student has just inserted a cannula on a ward. Which piece of feedback is most useful?

options.text: 'You checked the patient's identity and prepared the skin well; next time release the tourniquet as soon as the line is flushed.'
'Good job.'
'You are always clumsy.'
'Do it better next time.'

questions.correctOptionText: 'You checked the patient's identity and prepared the skin well; next time release the tourniquet as soon as the line is flushed.'

distractorRationale.c: A personal judgement that causes defensiveness.

questions.explanation: Effective feedback is specific, based on what was observed, balanced and tells the learner what to do next. Vague praise or personal criticism gives no information to act on.

questions.stem: A medical student you are supervising uses jargon and interrupts an anxious older patient while explaining a procedure. Describe how you would respond at the time and give feedback afterwards, naming the communication principles you would model.
markingGuide: Protect the patient first: gently step in or rephrase in plain language during the encounter without humiliating the student
Choose a private, timely moment for feedback
Ask the student to self-assess first (what went well, what they would change)
Give specific, behaviour-based feedback: examples of jargon and interruptions and their effect on the patient
Offer a concrete improvement plan such as chunking information, teach-back and open questions, and model them
Agree a way to observe again and follow up
Reinforce strengths and check the student's understanding
questions.explanation: The patient's welfare comes first and the feedback should be specific, private and constructive. Credit goes to showing how the teacher models plain language, open questions and teach-back and agrees a follow-up with the student.

questions.stem: A patient on your ward is medically fit but lives alone, has fallen twice recently and cannot manage the stairs at home. What is the best next step?

options.text: Discharge him today to free the bed and arrange a clinic follow-up
Ask the pharmacist to decide whether he can manage at home
Refer early to the physiotherapist and occupational therapist for functional assessment and involve the discharge coordinator or social worker
Wait for the family to raise any concerns

questions.correctOptionText: Refer early to the physiotherapist and occupational therapist for functional assessment and involve the discharge coordinator or social worker

distractorRationale.b: Outside the pharmacist's role for functional assessment.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: uses the multidisciplinary team to make discharge safe.
distractorRationale.d: Passive and risks an unsafe discharge.

questions.explanation: A safe discharge for a frail patient depends on function, equipment and support at home, which therapists and social care colleagues assess. Early referral prevents delay and readmission, and the doctor's role is to make a clear, timely request and document the plan.
